blocks.text: A reactor's feed temperature is measured upstream, and every time a cold batch arrives the outlet temperature dips for several minutes before the feedback loop notices and corrects it. The disturbance was visible a minute before it hurt. Feedforward uses that early warning to act in advance; feedback with a model of what the plant does not know keeps the loop honest when the prediction is imperfect.

blocks.markdown: Take a plant with a control input $u$ and a measured disturbance $d$. In the Laplace domain the output is $Y=G_p(s)U+G_d(s)D$, where $G_p$ is the plant transfer function from the input and $G_d$ the transfer function from the disturbance. **Feedback** reacts only after $d$ has moved $y$. **Feedforward** adds a term $U_{ff}=G_{ff}(s)D$ computed from the measured $d$ so that the disturbance is cancelled at the output before an error develops.

blocks.caption: Ideal feedforward: the combined disturbance path $G_d+G_pG_{ff}$ vanishes.

blocks.title: Conditions for feedforward
blocks.text: The ideal $G_{ff}=-G_d/G_p$ must be (i) proper (no more zeros than poles), (ii) stable, and (iii) free of right-half-plane zeros in $G_p$ that it would have to invert. It also needs the disturbance to be measured and the models $G_p$ and $G_d$ to be accurate. Residual error is proportional to the model error.

blocks.title: Feedforward for a thermal process
blocks.prompt: A heated process has $G_p(s)=\dfrac{2}{5s+1}$ (K per kW) and a measured ambient disturbance with $G_d(s)=\dfrac{0.8}{3s+1}$ (K per K). Find $G_{ff}$, check it is realisable, and find the residual if the true disturbance gain is 0.9 rather than 0.8.

steps.text: Realisability: numerator and denominator have the same degree, so it is proper (a lead term, zero at $0.2$ rad/s and pole at $0.33$ rad/s). The plant has no right-half-plane zero and the poles are stable.
Static check: at DC the feedforward gives $-0.4$ per unit disturbance, so the disturbance contributes $0.8-2\times0.4=0$.
If the true disturbance gain is 0.9, the same feedforward leaves a static residual.

blocks.answer: $G_{ff}=-0.4\,(5s+1)/(3s+1)$. A 12.5% error in the disturbance gain still leaves 0.1 of the unit disturbance (about 11% of its uncompensated effect), which feedback must then remove.

rows: Directly: accuracy of cancellation depends on it
Handles unmeasured disturbances and model error
blocks.caption: Feedback and feedforward are complementary: use feedforward for speed and feedback for robustness.

blocks.markdown: **Feedback rejection and sensitivity.** For an output disturbance with a loop $L=GC$, the output is $Y=S\,D_o$ with $S=1/(1+L)$. At a frequency $\omega$, $|S(j\omega)|$ is the factor by which the closed loop scales the disturbance relative to open loop. Where $|L|\gg1$ we have $|S|\approx1/|L|$, so high loop gain at the disturbance frequency means strong rejection.

blocks.title: Attenuation at one frequency
blocks.prompt: A loop has $L(j\omega)=4\angle-120^\circ$ at $\omega=2$ rad/s. Estimate how much a sinusoidal output disturbance at 2 rad/s is attenuated.

steps.text: The rough rule $|S|\approx1/|L|=0.25$ is close because $|L|$ is moderately large, but ignores the phase.

blocks.answer: $|S|\approx0.28$: the disturbance at 2 rad/s is reduced to about 28% of its open-loop amplitude (-11.1 dB).

blocks.markdown: **Why bandwidth is limited.** The model of the plant is only trustworthy up to some frequency. Beyond it there are unmodelled dynamics: flexible modes, sensor and actuator lags, computation and transport delays. Write the true plant as $G_p(1+\Delta_m)$, where $\Delta_m(j\omega)$ is the multiplicative error. A sufficient condition for robust stability is the small-gain test $|T(j\omega)|\,|\Delta_m(j\omega)|<1$ at all $\omega$, with $T=L/(1+L)$ the complementary sensitivity. Since $|T|\approx1$ up to the bandwidth and falls beyond, the loop bandwidth must lie below the frequency where $|\Delta_m|$ reaches 1.

blocks.title: A delay limits the bandwidth
blocks.prompt: An unmodelled actuator delay of 20 ms gives $\Delta_m=e^{-j\omega\tau}-1$. Estimate the frequency above which $|\Delta_m|\ge1$, and say what this implies for the crossover frequency.

steps.text: The magnitude of the error is $|e^{-j\omega\tau}-1|=2\sin(\omega\tau/2)$.
Since $|T|\approx1$ near crossover, the crossover frequency must stay well below this; a common rule of thumb is half or less.

blocks.answer: The error reaches 100% at about 52 rad/s, so the loop bandwidth should be kept to roughly 26 rad/s or lower.

blocks.title: The trade-off
blocks.text: Disturbance rejection wants $|L|$ large (hence $|S|$ small) over a wide band, but unmodelled dynamics force $|L|$ to fall below 1 before the uncertainty reaches 100%. Feedforward relieves the trade-off: it cancels a measured disturbance without needing high loop gain, so the bandwidth can stay modest.

blocks.title: Do not invert what you do not know
blocks.text: Feedforward inverts the plant. If $G_p$ has a right-half-plane zero or a delay, the exact inverse is unstable or non-causal, and if the model is wrong the cancellation is partial. Use the static part with confidence, the dynamic part with caution, and keep feedback in the loop.

points: Ideal feedforward from a measured disturbance is $G_{ff}=-G_d/G_p$; it must be proper and stable, and its accuracy depends on model accuracy, so feedback remains necessary.
For an output disturbance $Y=SD$, where $|L|\gg1$ the attenuation factor is $|S|\approx1/|L|$; evaluate $|1/(1+L)|$ exactly at the disturbance frequency.
Unmodelled dynamics (delays, resonances) grow with frequency and limit the loop bandwidth to well below the frequency at which the uncertainty reaches 100%.

questions.stem: For a plant $Y=G_pU+G_dD$ with a measured disturbance $D$, what is the ideal feedforward transfer function $G_{ff}$ (added to the input as $U=U_{fb}+G_{ff}D$)?

distractorRationale.a: Then $G_d+G_pG_{ff}=0$ and the disturbance has no effect on the output.
distractorRationale.b: The product does not cancel the disturbance path.
distractorRationale.c: This inverts the ratio; it would cancel only if the roles of the paths were reversed.
distractorRationale.d: A fixed gain cancels the disturbance only when the two paths happen to be identical and equal in size.

questions.explanation: The disturbance reaches the output through $G_d+G_pG_{ff}$, which is zero if $G_{ff}=-G_d/G_p$. The plant model must be inverted, so its accuracy limits the cancellation.

questions.stem: Why is feedback usually kept in the loop even when feedforward from a measured disturbance is applied?

options.text: Feedforward always makes the loop unstable
Feedforward is only as accurate as the models and cannot handle unmeasured disturbances
Feedforward needs a measurement of the output

questions.correctOptionText: Feedforward is only as accurate as the models and cannot handle unmeasured disturbances

distractorRationale.a: Feedforward sits outside the loop and does not change loop stability.
distractorRationale.b: Feedback corrects residual error from model mismatch and unmeasured effects.
distractorRationale.c: Cost is not the technical reason.
distractorRationale.d: It needs a measurement of the disturbance, not the output.

questions.explanation: Cancellation depends on knowing $G_p$ and $G_d$, and real plants have errors and other disturbances that no sensor measures. Feedback detects the leftover error and removes it.

questions.stem: At a frequency where $|L(j\omega)|=20$, which approximate value of $|S|$ applies?

distractorRationale.a: This would be the loop gain itself, not the sensitivity.
distractorRationale.b: $|S|\to1$ where the loop gain is small, not large.
distractorRationale.c: This would correspond to $|L|\approx1$ with a particular phase.

questions.explanation: $S=1/(1+L)$, and for $|L|\gg1$ the 1 in the denominator is negligible, so $|S|\approx1/|L|=0.05$, a 26 dB attenuation. A larger loop gain gives stronger rejection at that frequency.

questions.stem: Why must the closed-loop bandwidth be limited by unmodelled dynamics such as a flexible mode or a small delay?

options.text: The plant always has more gain at high frequency
The controller cannot be implemented above 1 Hz
Model error grows with frequency, and high loop gain where the plant is uncertain can destabilise the loop
High bandwidth reduces the disturbance rejection

questions.correctOptionText: Model error grows with frequency, and high loop gain where the plant is uncertain can destabilise the loop

distractorRationale.a: Most plants roll off at high frequency, which is why uncertainty is the real issue, not gain.
distractorRationale.b: There is no such fixed limit; implementation limits depend on the hardware.
distractorRationale.c: The small-gain condition needs $|T||\Delta_m|<1$, so $|T|$ must be small where $|\Delta_m|$ is large.
distractorRationale.d: Higher bandwidth usually improves rejection; the limit comes from uncertainty.

questions.explanation: Above some frequency the model is unreliable, so $|\Delta_m|$ is not small. To keep $|T||\Delta_m|<1$ the complementary sensitivity must fall before that frequency, which forces the bandwidth below it.

questions.stem: True or false: with a feedforward controller designed from a model whose disturbance gain is 20% too small, about 20% of the original disturbance effect remains after cancellation.
questions.explanation: If the model underestimates the disturbance path by 20% of its true gain, the cancelling signal removes 80% of the disturbance, so the residual is about 20% of the true effect. Feedback must remove this remainder.

questions.stem: A plant has static gain $G_p(0)=5$ and the disturbance path has static gain $G_d(0)=1.5$. Find the magnitude of the static feedforward gain $|G_{ff}(0)|=|G_d(0)/G_p(0)|$ (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: The ideal static gain is $G_d(0)/G_p(0)=1.5/5=0.3$, with a negative sign in the convention $U=U_{fb}-0.3D$. Then the static effect is $1.5-5\times0.3=0$.

questions.stem: At a frequency $\omega$ the open-loop frequency response of a loop is $L(j\omega)=3\angle-90^\circ$ (i.e. $-3j$). Find $|S(j\omega)|$ (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: $1+L=1-3j$ has magnitude $\sqrt{1+9}=3.162$, so $|S|=1/3.162=0.316$ (about $-10$ dB). The estimate $1/|L|=0.33$ is close.

questions.stem: An unmodelled delay of 8 ms gives multiplicative error $|\Delta_m|=2\sin(\omega\tau/2)$. Using the criterion $|\Delta_m|<1$, find the largest frequency, in rad/s, at which the error is still below 100%.
questions.explanation: The error equals 1 when $\sin(\omega\tau/2)=1/2$, i.e. $\omega\tau/2=\pi/6$, so $\omega=\pi/(3\tau)=\pi/(3\times0.008)=130.9$ rad/s. The crossover frequency should be kept well below this.

questions.stem: A process has $G_p(s)=\dfrac{4}{2s+1}$ and a measured disturbance path $G_d(s)=\dfrac{3}{6s+1}$. Design the ideal feedforward transfer function, state its static value and check realisability, and explain why feedback is still needed.
markingGuide: Realisable: numerator and denominator are both first order (proper) and the pole at $-1/6$ is stable, with no right-half-plane zero in $G_p$ to invert.
Feedback is still needed because model errors leave a residual and unmeasured disturbances cannot be cancelled.
questions.explanation: The ratio gives $G_{ff}=-0.75(2s+1)/(6s+1)$, with static value $-0.75$. It is proper and stable, so it can be implemented, but any error in $G_p$ or $G_d$ leaves a residual, and unmeasured disturbances are untouched, so feedback is retained.

questions.stem: A servo must attenuate a disturbance at 5 rad/s by a factor of 10 ($|S|\le0.1$). Its loop gain falls at $-20$ dB/decade near crossover, and an unmodelled resonance makes the model error reach 100% at 100 rad/s. Discuss the feasibility of the design using the crossover frequency, and suggest how feedforward could help.
markingGuide: With a $-20$ dB/decade slope the loop gain falls to 1 at about $5\times10=50$ rad/s, so the crossover must be at or above about 50 rad/s.
The uncertainty limit suggests crossover at about half of 100 rad/s or lower, i.e. $\lesssim50$ rad/s: the requirements just meet with no safety margin.
A steeper slope is not possible near crossover without losing phase margin; so the design is marginal.
Suggests feedforward of the measured disturbance (or reducing the requirement) so that less loop gain is needed.
questions.explanation: $|S|\le0.1$ at 5 rad/s needs $|L|\ge10$ there, and with a $-20$ dB/decade slope that puts the crossover at about 50 rad/s. The 100% model error at 100 rad/s only allows crossover at about 50 rad/s or lower, so the design is feasible only with no margin; feedforward from a measured disturbance would reduce the demand on feedback gain.
